messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

James, a 45-year-old African-American man, grew up in a small rural town where he witnessed severe domestic violence between his parents. The memory of those nights is still vivid; his father would come home drunk and hurl himself at his mother, yelling and hitting her until she cried out for help. James was certain that if he had been able to do more, the situation might have been different. This guilt has followed him into adulthood. James works on a farm, which offers little solace from his past. The isolation of working in open fields often triggers memories of those nights when his parents fought. He has come to believe that he is a miserable person who cannot trust anyone else, as if every interaction carries the potential for betrayal or harm. This belief has led him into a cycle of hypervigilance and rumination, with each experience reinforcing the other. During his workday, James is always alert, constantly scanning his surroundings to ensure that no one can sneak up on him or hurt him like he had seen happen so many times as a child. At night, when he lies in bed, it’s even harder for him to feel safe. The darkness intensifies his feelings of vulnerability and makes him question whether anyone can truly protect him. The hypervigilance has led James to avoid being alone with another person at all costs. He is convinced that if he lets down his guard, the same kind of violence might erupt again. This avoidance behavior, however, has strained his relationships. His wife often feels neglected and misunderstood, and their interactions are frequently punctuated by tension and misunderstanding. James tries hard not to think about those traumatic nights, but the memories persistently resurface during the quiet moments when he is alone on the farm or at home. He finds himself ruminating about how to exact revenge on his father, though he knows it’s an impossible wish. This rumination only deepens his feelings of guilt and despair, reinforcing his belief that life will never be happy again. The hypervigilance and avoidance behaviors have become self-reinforcing; the more James avoids situations where he might feel vulnerable, the stronger his negative appraisals about himself and others become. He has lost faith in people, believing that they are fundamentally untrustworthy, which makes it harder for him to let down his guard or seek help. What finally brought James to seek help was a recent incident at work where he overreacted to a minor disagreement with a coworker. The confrontation left both parties shaken, and his wife urged him to see a therapist. He is most afraid that his past will continue to control every aspect of his life, but he is also hoping for some relief from the constant fear and guilt that have become part of his daily existence. James’s journey towards healing starts with understanding how his childhood experiences shaped his current beliefs and behaviors, and working towards breaking the cycle that has kept him trapped in hypervigilance and despair.
